channel.title: The Hermeticum
channel.description: Serious history of the Hermetic tradition — real sources, no fortune-telling.

item.title: Start Here — a clear path into Hermeticism
item.description: A structured, honest introduction to the Hermetic tradition: what it is, what it isn't, and a twelve-step path from zero to reading the sources.

item.title: What is Hermeticism? The honest answer
item.description: Hermeticism explained honestly: ancient Greek-Egyptian texts, the Renaissance revival, occult orders and a 1908 book — four things, one word.

item.title: Who was Hermes Trismegistus?
item.description: Hermes Trismegistus was not a person but a literary persona fusing Greek Hermes and Egyptian Thoth — and the story of how a god became an author.

item.title: Alexandria — the world that made the Hermetica
item.description: The Hermetic texts were written in Roman Egypt, where Greek philosophy met a temple religion in decline. This is the world that produced them.

item.title: Corpus Hermeticum — guide to the treatises
item.description: The Corpus Hermeticum: seventeen Greek treatises from Roman Egypt — dating, contents, the 'missing Book XV' myth, and which translation to read.

item.title: Poimandres — the vision that opens the Corpus
item.description: Poimandres (Corpus Hermeticum I): the visionary cosmogony that opens the Hermetic corpus — summary, structure and how to read it without Greek.

item.title: The Emerald Tablet — the real origin
item.description: The Emerald Tablet is first attested in Arabic (8th-9th c.) — no Greek original, no emerald. The real history, the Latin text, Newton's own copy.

item.title: Asclepius — the perfect discourse
item.description: The Asclepius: the longest Hermetic treatise, surviving in Latin — 'man is a great miracle', the god-making passages, and the lament for Egypt.

item.title: The Kybalion — 1908, read with care
item.description: The Kybalion (1908) was written by W.W. Atkinson, not ancient masters. What its seven principles are, where they come from, how to read it honestly.

item.title: Hermes Trismegistus — the author who never lived
item.description: Hermes Trismegistus: the fusion of Greek Hermes and Egyptian Thoth, the persona behind the Hermetica, prophet in Islam, sage of the Renaissance.

item.title: As above, so below — what it actually means
item.description: 'As above, so below' comes from the Emerald Tablet's Latin — an 8th-9th c. Arabic text — and the famous wording is a 19th-century paraphrase.

item.title: Nous — the divine Mind
item.description: Nous in the Hermetica: the divine Mind that is both God's essence and humanity's deepest faculty — definition, sources and common misreadings.

item.title: About & Method — how The Hermeticum works
item.description: Our method: three layers — fact, scholarly debate, reception and myth — named sources with dates, honest gaps, corrections in the open.

item.title: Frances Yates — the thesis and its afterlife
item.description: Frances Yates and the Yates thesis: how her 1964 book on Giordano Bruno created "the Hermetic tradition" as a field — and how scholars took it apart.

item.title: Giordano Bruno — not the martyr you think
item.description: Why was Giordano Bruno burned at the stake in 1600? Not for Copernicanism — the charges were theological. The martyr-of-science myth, examined.

item.title: John Dee — the queen's mathematician-magus
item.description: John Dee (1527–1608/9): Elizabethan mathematician, author of the Monas Hieroglyphica, and diarist of "angel conversations" — facts vs. the 007 spy myth.

item.title: Lodovico Lazzarelli — the purest Hermetist
item.description: Lodovico Lazzarelli completed the Latin Corpus Hermeticum and actually lived its rebirth doctrine — the purest Christian Hermetist of the Renaissance.

item.title: Marsilio Ficino — the man who lit the fuse
item.description: Marsilio Ficino translated the Corpus Hermeticum into Latin in 1463 — before Plato, on Cosimo de' Medici's orders — and launched Renaissance Hermeticism.

item.title: Pico della Mirandola — the 900 theses
item.description: Pico della Mirandola, his 900 Theses, and why the famous Oration on the Dignity of Man was never delivered — and isn't the humanist manifesto you think.

item.title: Thoth — the god behind Hermes Trismegistus
item.description: Who was Thoth? Egypt's god of writing and reckoning, scribe of the gods at the weighing of the heart — and the origin of Hermes Trismegistus.

item.title: Zosimos of Panopolis — the first named alchemist
item.description: Zosimos of Panopolis (c. 300 CE): history's first alchemist known by name, his dream-visions of tormented metal men, and his link to the Hermetica.

item.title: Correspondences — the web of cosmic sympathy
item.description: Correspondences in Hermetic thought: cosmic sympathy linking heaven, earth and humanity — the ancient sources, and why the famous tables are much later.

item.title: Gnosis — knowledge that transforms the knower
item.description: Gnosis in the Hermetica: salvific knowledge of God that deifies the knower — where the texts say it, how it differs from Gnosticism and 'secret knowledge'.

item.title: Hermeticism vs Gnosticism & the rest
item.description: How Hermeticism relates to Gnosticism, Platonism, Stoicism, Kabbalah and Christianity — real historical kinships versus modern look-alikes.

item.title: Palingenesia — rebirth in Corpus Hermeticum XIII
item.description: Palingenesia in CH XIII: rebirth as ten divine powers expelling twelve zodiacal torments — liberation from astral fate in this life, not reincarnation.

item.title: Prisca theologia — the first-wisdom myth
item.description: Prisca theologia: the Renaissance belief that Hermes taught an ancient theology older than Plato — its rise with Ficino, its fall with Casaubon in 1614.

item.title: The Great Work — what alchemists actually did
item.description: The Great Work (magnum opus): the alchemists' staged process for making the philosophers' stone — the color stages, the lost yellow, and the Jung problem.

item.title: The Ogdoad and Ennead — the Eighth and the Ninth
item.description: The Ogdoad and Ennead: the Eighth and Ninth spheres of Hermetic ascent in CH I and Nag Hammadi — and why they differ from Egypt's Ennead of nine gods.

item.title: Theurgy — ritual ascent to the divine
item.description: Theurgy: the late-antique ritual path to union with the divine, defended by Iamblichus and Proclus — and its real relation to the Hermetic writings.

item.title: Reading Poimandres — a guided first source
item.description: Read Poimandres (Corpus Hermeticum I) with a guide: the vision, the cosmogony, the fall of the Human and the ascent through the spheres — plainly explained.

item.title: Definitions of Hermes — the oldest Hermetic text
item.description: The Definitions of Hermes to Asclepius: probably the oldest Hermetic text, preserved in Armenian and first translated into English in 1999.

item.title: Musaeum Hermeticum — the 1625 anthology
item.description: The Musaeum Hermeticum (Frankfurt 1625, expanded 1678): a Baroque anthology of 21 alchemical treatises — with no ancient Hermetica inside.

item.title: Nag Hammadi Hermetica — the 1945 desert find
item.description: Three Hermetic texts found in the Egyptian desert in 1945 — including the ritual Discourse on the Eighth and Ninth. What the find changed.

item.title: Picatrix — the Arabic handbook of astral magic
item.description: The Picatrix (Ghayat al-Hakim): a 10th-century Arabic manual of astral magic from al-Andalus that shaped Renaissance magic via Alfonso X's court.

item.title: Stobaean Fragments — the Kore Kosmou
item.description: The Stobaean fragments: nearly thirty Hermetic excerpts saved in a 5th-century anthology, including the Kore Kosmou — Isis teaching Horus.
